title: Global climate concern is translating into demand for faster action, protection and cooperation, but the political meaning of that demand is shaped by lived exposure, fairness and trust in delivery
source_unit: United Nations Development Programme, University of Oxford and GeoPoll, Peoples' Climate Vote 2024
geography: Public attitudes across 77 countries representing 87 percent of the world's population, with regional and demographic comparisons

observations.period: 2023–2024; global climate concern and government action

denominator.unit: people surveyed across 77 countries in the Peoples' Climate Vote 2024

stronger_action.unit: percent of people globally wanting their country to take stronger action on climate change

more_worried.unit: percent of people globally saying they are more worried about climate change than the previous year

action_signal.value: climate concern is broad and is accompanied by demand for stronger government action

observations.method: GeoPoll computer-assisted telephone interviews conducted from September 2023 to May 2024 for UNDP, with analysis by the University of Oxford; the survey covered 15 climate questions across 77 countries.
observations.uncertainty: The survey measures reported attitudes rather than policy compliance, emissions reduction, willingness to pay, or realized political behavior; country and regional precision varies with sample size and weighting.
observations.subgroup: Adults across surveyed countries, voters, households, workers and communities experiencing climate impacts or evaluating government response.
observations.counterinterpretation: Demand for stronger action may coexist with disagreement over policy instruments, timing, distributional costs and which institutions should act.

denominator.unit: Peoples' Climate Vote 2024 respondents across 77 countries

fossil_fuel_exit.unit: percent of people globally wanting their country to move away from fossil fuels to clean energy quickly

nature_protection.unit: percent of people globally wanting more protection for people at risk from extreme weather

policy_direction.value: support extends beyond abstract concern to faster clean-energy transition and protection from climate harms

observations.method: Cross-country descriptive analysis of the Peoples' Climate Vote 2024 responses on fossil-fuel transition and protection from extreme weather.
observations.uncertainty: Support for a direction of travel does not identify preferred policy design, acceptable household cost, local siting preference, or willingness to change personal behavior.
observations.subgroup: Households, energy consumers, workers in fossil and clean-energy sectors, climate-exposed people and governments setting energy policy.
observations.counterinterpretation: A rapid transition can be broadly popular while particular taxes, bans, infrastructure projects or job losses remain politically contested.

observations.period: 2023–2024; climate exposure, daily life and unequal vulnerability

denominator.unit: Peoples' Climate Vote 2024 respondents across 77 countries

life_decisions.unit: percent of people globally saying climate change has impacted major life decisions such as where they work or live

worsening_extreme_weather.unit: percent of people globally thinking extreme weather events have gotten worse

unequal_exposure.value: people in least developed countries and small island developing states report especially high salience and worry about climate change

observations.method: Descriptive comparison of reported climate experience, life decisions, extreme-weather perceptions and country-group patterns.
observations.uncertainty: Reported experience and perception are not equivalent to meteorological exposure or causal relocation, employment or migration effects; country-group differences may reflect sampling, context and question interpretation.
observations.subgroup: People in least developed countries, small island developing states, climate-exposed households, workers and communities making place or livelihood decisions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Climate salience can reflect media, local events and political communication as well as direct exposure, and high concern does not prove that climate change is the dominant driver of a life decision.

denominator.unit: Peoples' Climate Vote 2024 respondents across 77 countries

cooperation.unit: percent of people globally wanting countries to set aside geopolitical differences and work together on climate change

rich_country_adaptation.unit: percent of people globally wanting richer countries to help poorer countries adapt

legitimacy_route.value: climate cooperation is linked in public demand to fairness between countries and support for vulnerable populations

observations.method: Cross-country descriptive analysis of responses on geopolitical cooperation, adaptation responsibility and climate action.
observations.uncertainty: Stated support for cooperation and adaptation finance does not establish fiscal willingness, diplomatic behavior, aid delivery, or agreement over burden-sharing formulas.
observations.subgroup: People in climate-vulnerable countries, citizens of higher-income countries, governments, international institutions and communities seeking adaptation finance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Global cooperation can be publicly desirable while domestic political incentives, budget constraints and geopolitical conflict obstruct implementation.

related_sources.claim: Official methodology, fieldwork dates, weighting and country-level margin-of-error notes.

boundary: This record adds a global public-meaning and legitimacy layer to the energy and just-transition sequence. It is a cross-country attitude survey, not respondent-level causal evidence, a measure of policy compliance, a local siting referendum, a climate-exposure dataset, or proof that stated support becomes durable political action.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official UNDP publication page, full report PDF, UNDP explainer, UN results page and methodology page were reviewed for sample frame, action demand, fossil-fuel transition, life decisions, extreme-weather perception, adaptation responsibility and geopolitical cooperation; the full report PDF was hashed.
